newsitem.title: USA: USDA SEEN HIKING U.S. WHEAT OUTPUT, CUTTING CORN.
newsitem.headline: USDA SEEN HIKING U.S. WHEAT OUTPUT, CUTTING CORN.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department's August crop production report slated for release at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT Tuesday is expected to show an increase in the estimate of 1997 U.S. wheat production but a decrease in 1997 U.S. corn output, analysts said.
USDA in July pegged the 1997 U.S. corn crop at 9.7 billion bushels. But an average of analysts' estimates indicated the USDA's August report Tuesday will come in at 9.554 billion.
"Obviously we'll be coming down," said Dan Cekander, Chicago-based analyst for FIMAT Futures.
"The USDA July estimate was based on good yields but it's been dry since so we have to ratchet down yields," Cekander said.
FIMAT's corn output estimate was 9.546 billion bushels.
Some forecasters predicted corn production would hold roughly even with the government's outlook in July.

"I don't think some people realize how tough these new varieties and hybrids are," said Sid Love, of Joe Kropf and Sid Love Consulting, Kansas City. Love, who last week toured key corn growing areas of the U.S., pegged the 1997 corn crop at 9.771 billion bushels which was the top of the range of estimates.
"I really trashed (reduced) Illinois, Missouri and Nebraska (corn) yields but Iowa and Minnesota are just screaming record yields," said ADM Investor Services' chief grain analyst Steve Freed.

Dry weather in the U.S. Midwest this summer was most serious in Illinois, Missouri and Nebraska but most of Iowa and all of Minnesta have received adequate rainfall. Freed said he used average trendline yields to compute his corn crop projection in the eastern corn belt, including Indiana and Ohio.
ADM's corn production outlook was 9.6 billion bushels.

An average of analysts' estimates pegged U.S. wheat production at 2.476 billion bushels, above the government's forecast in July for 2.431 billion. The increase was expected to show up in the winter wheat category.
"Everybody is hearing the same thing, the winter wheat is underestimated by USDA," Freed said.

In St. Louis, Doane Agriculture Services wheat specialist Bill Nelson said he increased his estimate of 1997 U.S. winter wheat after hearing of good wheat yields in the northern states of Nebraska, South Dakota, Ohio and Michigan.
"The wheat crop keeps getting bigger," Nelson said.

Spring wheat production also was expected to be above USDA's July outlook. An average of 10 analysts pegged spring wheat production in the U.S. this year at 589 million bushels, above USDA's July forecast for 569.265 million bushels.
Durum production was pegged by the analysts at 88 million bushels, above USDA's July outlook for 80.927 million bushels.
